text: Ricco (October 13, 1915 – March 27, 1972), born Erich Wassmer, was a Swiss painter known for depicting idealizing dream worlds in the genre of magic realism. Erich Wassmer was born in Allschwil into an upper-class environment as the son of cement factory owner and art patron Max Wassmer (1887–1970). From the age of three, he lived at Bremgarten Castle near Bern, a home rich in art and culture, where his parents socialized with notable figures such as Hermann Hesse, Louis Moilliet, Cuno Amiet, Paul Basilius Barth, and Othmar Schoeck. Early on, Erich developed an interest in painting, which the family supported due to the continued success of the family’s cement factory, secured by his two brothers. In 1937, he adopted the name Ricco—described as a "magic word"—to sign his works, replacing his father’s well-known industrialist identity. Ricco studied in Munich and Paris under Cuno Amiet, though the influence of his teachers was minimal. He was deeply fascinated by the sea and the idea of exploring lost paradises and uncharted territories, and he had an anchor tattooed on his arm, which he later incorporated into his signature. During the 1940s, he traveled by freighter across the ocean and lived in Tahiti. In the 1950s, he settled at Bompré Castle near Vichy. In 1963, French police discovered in his studio photographs of nude boys that served as the basis for his paintings. A French court convicted him—without a formal indictment—of sexual "exploitation" of young boys and breach of morality, sentencing him to eight months in prison. Ricco never fully recovered from this imprisonment. After his release, he returned to Switzerland and settled in a mansion in Ropraz, where he died in 1972 at the age of 56. Until his death, Ricco Wassmer remained a family shareholder in Portland-Cement-Werke AG. His early works, such as paintings of castle life, are classified as primitivist, while his mature work includes still lifes, harbor scenes, exotic motifs, and allegorical figures. He frequently painted dream worlds in the style of magic realism, featuring lean boys in surreal arrangements, reflecting his longing for androgynous, youthful perfection. His work is described as being rooted in everyday reality but possessing overtones of fantasy or wonder, creating a surreal atmosphere.
